episodes.159560: A small short wave trough overriding a very warm and rather humid air mass lead to late afternoon and evening pulse thunderstorms with damaging winds and large hail.
episodes.159561: Late afternoon thunderstorms that developed along the sea breeze collision produced strong wind gusts along the Brevard County coast.
episodes.159631: A west to east oriented line of thunderstorms evolved north of ON-401 through the afternoon hours on August 7. This line eventually evolved into a bit of a bowing segment as it took on a more northeast to southwest orientation during the evening hours while crossing the St. Lawrence Valley. This resulted in downed trees on Grindstone Island.
episodes.159657: Scattered thunderstorms developed in the late afternoon and evening hours in a warm and unstable airmass.
episodes.159659: Scattered thunderstorms developed in the late afternoon and evening hours in a warm and unstable airmass.
episodes.159717: A midlevel shortwave trough trekked across the region. This feature tapped into residual moisture to produce scattered showers and thunderstorms. The stronger storms produced gusty winds in excess of 58 mph across portions of western Colorado.
episodes.159740: Several strong thunderstorms affected the nearshore and shore areas of Lake Michigan from Sheboygan south to Kenosha during the late afternoon on August 6th.
episodes.160304: Several severe thunderstorms impacted portions of southern Wisconsin, especially near Lake Michigan as storms developed across central Wisconsin and eventually morphed into a line that dropped south into Illinois.
episodes.160305: A few supercell thunderstorms developed over western Wisconsin and move east into southern Wisconsin. These eventually morphed into more of a thunderstorm complex as they entered southern Wisconsin. Strong to severe storms caused pockets of wind damage and a tornado.
episodes.160659: Scattered afternoon thunderstorms developed across East Tennessee, a few of which produced large hail and damaging wind gusts.
episodes.160660: Scattered afternoon thunderstorms developed across southwest Virginia, one of which produced large hail.
episodes.160896: A complex of storms generated locally severe winds of up to over 70 mph before weakening and moving to the east during the late evening hours.
episodes.160919: A cluster of severe thunderstorms tracked across far southwestern into south central South Dakota during the late afternoon and early evening hours. The storms produced small hail and wind gusts of 60 to 70 mph across portions of the area.
episodes.160926: A thunderstorm briefly became severe over northeastern Pennington County, producing wind gusts to 70 mph.
episodes.161058: Scattered thunderstorms moved across southern Lake Michigan during the evening of August 6th.
episodes.161541: A couple of fair weather waterspouts were spotted off the coast of Horry County near North Myrtle Beach, SC.
episodes.161606: Thunderstorms developed across southeast Minnesota during the late morning of August 7th and continued into the early afternoon. Some of these storms dropped up to quarter sized hail on the north side of Rochester (Olmsted County) and near Goodview (Winona County). Locally heavy rains from the storms caused some street flooding to occur in Goodview and the west side of Winona (Winona County).
episodes.161607: Several rounds of storms moved across western Wisconsin during the afternoon of August 7th. One of these storms produced an EF3 tornado that started in Boscobel (Grant County) and traveled east/southeast before dissipating south of Blue River (Grant County). Along the path of the tornado, 6 homes sustained enough damage to be considered total losses but no injuries occurred. Flash flooding caused a mud slide along State Highway 33 southeast of La Crosse (La Crosse County) and washed out part of County Road NN south of St. Joseph (La Crosse County). Water also covered portions of State Highway 27 and County Roads J and X near Melvina (Monroe County). Coon Creek went out of its banks and caused extensive damage to the baseball field in Coon Valley (Vernon County). A county wide disaster was declared by Vernon County officials because of the flood damage.
episodes.161691: Scattered thunderstorms developed in the evening across parts of the Sandhills. An isolated severe thunderstorm moved across parts of Sheridan into Cherry counties in the evening.
episodes.161727: A strong upper level disturbance moved over the Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles causing thunderstorms to form. These thunderstorms moved from west to east with the greatest coverage occurring across the northern combined Panhandles. Moderate instability and weak wind shear were sufficient to support hail upwards of an inch and few severe wind gusts up to 60-70 mph in a few storms.
episodes.161728: A strong upper level disturbance moved over the Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles causing thunderstorms to form. These thunderstorms moved from west to east with the greatest coverage occurring across the northern combined Panhandles. Moderate instability and weak wind shear were sufficient to support hail upwards of an inch and few severe wind gusts up to 60-70 mph in a few storms.
episodes.161921: The axis of an upper trough crossed over northwestern NC during the afternoon of August 7. This trough combined with an unstable airmass helped trigger scattered thunderstorms. A few of these storms became severe producing damaging winds and large hail.
episodes.161933: On the evening of August 6th, a cold front moved into eastern Colorado and allowed thunderstorms to develop ahead of the front in east-central Colorado. These thunderstorms produced wind gusts up to 70 mph.
episodes.161962: Northeast Ohio was in a humid warm sector during the early evening of the 7th as the region remained well-south of a stationary front draped east-northeastward across southern Lake Michigan, central Lower Michigan, and southern Ontario. Forcing for ascent ahead of an eastward-moving mesoscale convective vortex and daytime heating-related boundary layer destabilization led to the development of isolated showers and thunderstorms in northeast Ohio during the early evening. A thunderstorm produced damaging wind gusts on the southwest side of Canfield as the storm encountered moderate MUCAPE and DCAPE, respectively, and weak effective bulk shear.
episodes.161981: The 24-hour period between the early mornings of Saturday the 7th and Sunday the 8th featured several rounds of thunderstorms within South Central Nebraska. However, by far the most prominent round focused between 6-10 p.m. CDT, during which time a burst of fairly widespread strong to severe activity affected mainly the southeast half of the area...especially east of a line from Franklin-St. Paul-Fullerton. Although ground-truth reports were somewhat limited considering that 16 Severe Thunderstorm Warnings were issued during these four hours, there were a handful of hail reports up to golf ball size along with a few mesonet-measured severe wind gusts (including 68 MPH near Lawrence and 63 MPH near Polk). A few of the more notable hail reports included: golf ball size near Giltner and Lawrence; ping pong ball size near Fairfield. Within the Tri Cities, parts of both Grand Island and Hastings observed small hail up to dime-nickel size, but for Grand Island the bigger story was actually heavy rain and a few rounds of fairly minor urban flooding as multiple storms cumulatively dumped a widespread 2-3 inches of rain within a bullseye centered directly over the city. However, the overall heaviest rain within South Central Nebraska actually concentrated within a southwest-northeast swath through the heart of Polk County, where amounts of 2.50-3.50 were common (including 3.35 in Osceola). Meanwhile, the vast majority of the 24-county area observed much lower and highly-variable rain amounts ranging from only a few hundredths up to around 1.50. ||Breaking down event evolution/timing and meteorological background, weak/non-severe convection percolated over much of South Central Nebraska throughout much of  the morning and afternoon, downstream from a seasonably-potent mid level shortwave trough slowly approaching from the NE/WY/CO border area. However, this activity diminished enough by late afternoon to allow considerable instability to build, aided by surface temperatures climbing into the mid-80s to around 90 (F) in the presence of healthy dewpoints mainly upper 60s-low 70s. By 6 p.m. CDT, the resultant mesoscale environment featured a fairly potent combination of 3000-4000 J/kg mixed-layer CAPE and 30-35 knots of deep-layer wind shear. Despite a lack of prominent surface boundaries within the area (only a fairly weak trough axis), the first initially-isolated strong-to-severe local storms of the day flared up between 6-7:30 p.m. CDT, one over Polk County (which dumped quarter size hail in Osceola) and another that lifted north out of Kansas into Webster/Nuckolls counties. Then, the ensuing few hours saw quite an uptick in the coverage of strong to severe storms within several central/eastern local counties. By around 10 p.m. CDT this activity quickly weakened below severe limits and started gradually departing off to the east. However, with a modest low level jet acting upon lingering elevated instability, additional flare-ups of spotty strong to perhaps marginally-severe storms (unverified) occurred mainly 1-4 a.m. CDT on the 8th, with a few of the most intense cells over Webster and Hall counties. Once this late-night round weakened/dissipated, most all of South Central Nebraska was finally convection-free by 5:30 a.m. CDT.
episodes.161982: The 24-hour period between the early mornings of Saturday the 7th and Sunday the 8th featured several rounds of thunderstorms within this six-county North Central Kansas area. However, by far the most noteworthy round focused between 6-9 p.m. CDT, during which time a burst of strong to severe activity roamed various parts of the local domain. Although ground-truth reports were somewhat limited, several mesonets clocked wind gusts up to around 55 MPH, with one severe-criteria gust of 66 MPH in Jewell. As for hail, although radar data suggested several cores possibly containing severe criteria stones, the only verifying report consisted of quarter size hail on the south side of Smith Center. ||Breaking down event evolution/timing and meteorological background, weak/non-severe convection percolated within North Central Kansas throughout much of the morning into early afternoon, downstream from a seasonably-potent mid level shortwave trough slowly approaching from the WY/CO border area. However, this activity diminished in plenty of time to allow several hours of heating and resultant instability to build, aided by surface temperatures climbing into the mid-90s to around 100 (F) in the presence of dewpoints mainly in the 60s. By 6 p.m. CDT, the resultant mesoscale environment featured a fairly potent combination of 2000-3000 J/kg mixed-layer CAPE and 30-35 knots of deep-layer wind shear. Between 6-7 p.m. CDT, the first strong to severe storms of the day rapidly flared up within the area, with initiation mainly focused along a south-southwest to north-northeast oriented surface trough. Over the next few hours, strong to severe convection continued within the area (including the early stages of a linear MCS that mainly affected Jewell/Mitchell counties), but by 9 p.m. CDT the vast majority of local activity had departed the local area either northward into Nebraska or eastward into northeast Kansas. Although a few additional flare-ups of spotty, weak convection occurred several hours later during the pre-dawn hours of the 8th, the aforementioned robust activity during the late afternoon-early evening of the 7th was by far the main event of the period.
episodes.162010: Light winds, high moisture, and an early morning land breeze led to conditions favorable for waterspouts across coastal waters.
episodes.162049: On August 7th, a lee-side trough moved from the front range of the Rocky Mountains into eastern Colorado which allowed severe thunderstorms to develop in east-central Colorado during the afternoon hours. These thunderstorms produced hail up to a half dollar in size.
episodes.162050: On August 7th, a lee-side trough moved from the front range of the Rocky Mountains into northwestern Kansas which allowed severe thunderstorms to develop in the area during the afternoon and evening hours. These thunderstorms produced hail up to 3.5-inch diameter in size and wind gusts up to 60 mph.
episodes.162085: A severe thunderstorm produced intense wind gusts to 65 mph.
episodes.162086: A severe thunderstorm produced large hail, up to half dollar size, in eastern Lincoln County.
episodes.162125: Thunderstorms initially developed across Nebraska along a cold front and aided by the low level jet before spreading across Iowa after midnight on the morning of August 8th. While instability was more than sufficient at 2500-3000 J/kg, shear prevent further organization and maintained an MCS storm mode. A small hail report and brief strong wind gust occurred with some sites getting two to five inches of rain, the storms generally remained below severe limits.
episodes.162218: An MCV moved across the area during afternoon peak heating. Isolated severe storms with downburst winds, hail, and localized flooding.
episodes.162233: A midlevel shortwave moved through the area producing storms with severe criteria hail and wind gusts. In Omaha, 2 to 3 inches of rain fell over about an hour which led to a flash flood warning being issued. Flash flooding washed through basement apartments, swept up cars, and heaved pavement in low-lying areas of the Omaha metro area. The City of Omaha Public Works office estimates the damage to the city near $1.10M.
episodes.162245: Scattered thunderstorms developed and moved slowly west across southeast Arizona. Large hail was reported near Rio Rico with flash flooding of Arivaca Rd. in northwest Santa Cruz and southeast Pima counties.
episodes.162404: Scattered showers and thunderstorms associated with low pressure moving from North Carolina northeast across Southeast Virginia and off the coast produced heavy rain which caused flooding and flash flooding across portions of central and eastern Virginia.
episodes.162443: Scattered showers and thunderstorms associated with low pressure moving from North Carolina northeast across Southeast Virginia and off the coast produced heavy rain which caused flooding across portions of the Lower Maryland Eastern Shore.
episodes.162444: Scattered thunderstorms associated with low pressure moving from North Carolina northeast across Southeast Virginia and off the coast produced a weak tornado across portions of southeast Virginia.
episodes.162603: Despite high pressure being in place, a boundary located just east of the Appalachians was able to advect enough moisture into the state for afternoon shower and thunderstorms to develop. These storms were scattered across eastern Kentucky, but were not strong enough to warrant any Severe Thunderstorm Warnings. The one exception was a storm that moved through portions of Harlan County, which was the strongest storm of the evening. This storm did result in a tree down just north of Harlan, the county seat.
episodes.162636: Scattered thunderstorms and storm clusters developed along the Blue Ridge escarpment during the early afternoon and moved steadily southeast. One of the storms produced damaging downburst winds in the Marion area.
episodes.162642: Widely scattered thunderstorms developed across the mountains during the afternoon. One of the storms produced brief damaging winds in Rabun County, Georgia.
episodes.162652: A cluster of thunderstorms moving from southeast South Dakota into northwest Iowa intensified briefly with the help from an increasing low-level jet, tapping elevated instability of up to 2000 J/kg. Linear organization led to a brief wind enhancement.
episodes.162727: An isolated thunderstorm that formed along a weak cold front near the Connecticut River briefly became severe when straight line winds knocked down some trees in Lisbon.
episodes.162736: Scattered severe storms rumbled across much of the CWA and produced large hail and damaging winds. Enhanced mid-level flow gave way to sufficient vertical shear with more organized convection, although more high based than further to the north.
episodes.162760: An upper level trough axis moved into western New York during the evening hours. This feature moved into a modestly unstable environment fairly unimpressive precipitable water values of only just slightly over one inch. Further, low level moisture transport was unimpressive. A cluster of storms congealed around northern Livingston and southern Monroe counties. Weak flow and some back-building allowed for torrential rain over the area. A few spots had three inches per hour rainfall rates that lasted up to 55 minutes.  This resulted in roads closed with water flowing over them in Monroe County.
episodes.162908: Training showers and storms developed along a stalled surface boundary, that was diabatically reinforced by widespread early day convection and resultant overcast skies. This coupled with a passing mid level disturbances allowed for multiple hours of heavy rain over Wayne County in central North Carolina, which resulted in several reports of flash flooding.
